title: Weighing the Earth
teaches: How a mountain and a pair of lead balls measured the Earth's density, and why that density demands a dense core

parts.title: A plumb line on a mountain

blocks.text: Newton's law of gravitation, published in 1687, says that every mass pulls on every other, with a force that grows with the masses and weakens with distance. It has a consequence that occupied scientists for nearly a century. A mountain should pull a plumb line (a weight hanging on a string) slightly sideways, toward itself. How far depends on how strongly the mountain pulls compared with the whole Earth beneath it. Each one's pull depends on its mass, which is its density times its volume. The volumes can be measured, so if you measure the lean and estimate the mountain's density, you can work out the density of the planet.

The effect is tiny. In 1774 the Astronomer Royal, Nevil Maskelyne, chose Schiehallion, a mountain in the Scottish Highlands, for the attempt, because its long east-west ridge is unusually regular and isolated, so its shape and pull could be calculated. He spent about four months camped on its slopes, first on the south side and then the north, measuring the positions of stars near overhead against a plumb line. The mountain pulled the line north at the south station and south at the north station. From the stars, each station's latitude could be worked out as if the plumb line hung truly; surveyors measured the real distance between the stations on the ground. The star latitudes differed by more than the survey said they should, and the difference was the two leans added together: 11.6 seconds of arc. A second of arc is a 3,600th of a degree, so this is about a third of a hundredth of a degree.

The mathematician Charles Hutton did the calculation. He needed the mountain's volume, so he took the surveyors' thousands of height measurements and drew lines joining points of equal height. Each line outlines a horizontal slice of the mountain, and adding up the slices gives the volume. These were the first **contour lines** used for land height, now on every topographic map. The lean was a little over half of what it would have been if the Earth were no denser than the mountain, so the Earth had to be about 1.8 times as dense as the mountain's rock. Assuming that rock was 2.5 grams per cubic centimetre, he got 4.5 for the Earth.

blocks.caption: Plumb lines on each side of Schiehallion. The mountain's pull is fixed; the denser the whole Earth, the harder it pulls straight down, and the less the lines lean. The lean is drawn 4,000 times larger than life.
blocks.task: Find the Earth density that gives Maskelyne's 11.6 seconds of arc

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A mountain pulls a plumb line sideways, by an amount that depends on its density compared with the whole Earth's.
Maskelyne measured a total deflection of 11.6 seconds of arc at Schiehallion in 1774.
Hutton calculated an Earth density of about 4.5 g/cm³, drawing early contour lines along the way.

blocks.text: Hutton's answer was only as good as his guess at the density of the mountain. In 1797 and 1798 Henry Cavendish removed the mountain from the problem. Using an apparatus designed by the clergyman and natural philosopher John Michell, who had died before he could use it, he hung a wooden rod with a small lead ball at each end from a fine wire, and set two large lead balls, about 158 kilograms each, beside the small ones. Their gravity pulled the small balls toward them and twisted the wire a little. How fast the rod swung back and forth told him how stiff the wire was, and so how much force each bit of twist meant; from that he worked out the tiny force between balls whose masses he knew.

Comparing that force with the pull of the whole Earth on the same balls, which is just their weight, and allowing for the Earth's radius of 6,371 kilometres, gave the Earth's mass, and so its density: 5.45 grams per cubic centimetre (his paper printed 5.48, an arithmetic slip found later). The modern value is 5.51. Rock at the Earth's surface averages about 2.7. The planet as a whole is twice as dense as the rock we stand on.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Cavendish measured the gravity between lead balls in 1798 and found the Earth's density to be about 5.45 g/cm³ (modern value 5.51).
Surface rock averages about 2.7 g/cm³, so the Earth as a whole is twice as dense as its crust.

blocks.text: Part of the answer is squeezing. Rock deep down is compressed by the weight above, so it is denser than the same rock at the surface. But laboratory measurements of how much rock compresses showed that squeezing alone falls short. Something heavier than rock must lie inside, and the obvious candidate was iron. Most meteorites that people had seen fall are stony, but some are almost pure iron mixed with nickel, as if they were pieces of the cores of broken planets.

A second measurement says how the mass is arranged. The Earth's axis is not fixed: it slowly sweeps around a cone, once every 26,000 years, a motion called **precession**, because the Sun and Moon tug on the Earth's equatorial bulge. The tug is known, so how fast the axis sweeps reveals how hard the Earth is to turn, its **moment of inertia**, and that depends on how far its mass sits from the centre, as a spinning skater turns slower with arms out than tucked in. A ball of the same density throughout would have a moment of inertia of 0.4 (in units of its mass times its radius squared); a ball with all its mass at the centre, 0. The Earth's is 0.331, so its mass is concentrated toward the middle.

blocks.caption: A two-layer Earth: a core and a mantle. Set the core's size and density; the mantle takes whatever density keeps the whole Earth at Cavendish's 5.5. The gauge shows how far from the centre the mass sits.
blocks.task: Find a core that fits both the density and the moment of inertia

blocks.text: In 1897 the German physicist Emil Wiechert put the two numbers together and proposed that the Earth has an iron core, of density about 8, reaching about three-quarters of the way out from the centre, under a rocky mantle of about 3.2. The idea was right and the numbers were not far off: the real core reaches a little over halfway out from the centre, and is denser, about 11 on average. Within a few years seismologists would find that core directly, by listening for the waves that earthquakes send through it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Compression of rock cannot account for all of the Earth's density; something heavier lies inside.
The moment of inertia, 0.331, shows the Earth's mass is concentrated toward the centre.
Wiechert proposed an iron core in 1897; the core's radius is just over half the Earth's.

blocks.caption: Five questions on weighing the Earth
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why did Maskelyne's plumb lines lean toward Schiehallion?
choices: The mountain's gravity pulled the bob sideways
Wind on the summit pushed the lines
The Earth's spin swung the lines toward the mountain
items.why: Every mass attracts every other. The mountain's pull added a small sideways force to the Earth's downward pull.

items.ask: If the Earth were the same size but much denser, how would the plumb line on Schiehallion lean?
choices: Less, because the Earth would pull harder downward compared with the mountain's sideways pull
More, because a denser Earth would make the mountain heavier
The same, because the deflection depends only on the mountain
items.why: The lean measures the mountain's pull against the whole Earth's. A stronger downward pull leaves the sideways one a smaller share.

items.ask: What did Cavendish's experiment measure that Maskelyne's could not do without a guess?
choices: The gravity between known masses, so no estimate of a mountain's density was needed
The speed of the Earth's rotation
items.why: Hutton's answer depended on an assumed density for Schiehallion. Cavendish's lead balls had known masses.

items.ask: The Earth averages 5.5 g/cm³; surface rock averages 2.7. What does that imply?
choices: Much denser material, more than compressed rock can explain, lies inside
items.why: Compression raises rock's density with depth, but not enough. A dense iron core makes up the difference.

items.ask: Why does the Earth's moment of inertia (0.331, against 0.4 for an even ball) point to a dense core?
choices: A value below 0.4 means mass is concentrated toward the centre
A value below 0.4 means the Earth is mostly covered in water
A value below 0.4 means the crust is denser than the mantle
items.why: An evenly dense ball gives 0.4; putting more mass near the centre lowers the number. The Earth's 0.331 needs a heavy centre.

learned: Maskelyne's plumb lines on Schiehallion (1774), worked through by Hutton, gave the first estimate of the Earth's density, about 4.5 g/cm³.
Cavendish's lead balls (1798) gave 5.45 g/cm³; the modern value is 5.51, twice that of surface rock.
The moment of inertia shows the mass is concentrated toward the centre, which requires a dense, probably iron, core.
